screens.title: What raise Does and When to Use It
screens.narratorSegment: The raise statement tells Python to stop normal execution and create an exception object representing an error you determined has occurred. Use raise when a function receives inputs or conditions that violate the intended contract. For example, a square root function should not proceed with negative inputs; raising ValueError makes the function's expectation explicit. When you raise a built-in exception, you can include a short explanatory message to help callers and debuggers understand what happened. A common pattern is input validation at the start of a function: check types and ranges, then raise TypeError or ValueError as appropriate. Why this matters: without explicit raises your code might continue into invalid states and cause misleading errors later, making bugs harder to trace. A common misconception is treating raise as only for catastrophic failures; in reality, it's the right tool for predictable, catchable problems. Example: if a function expects a positive integer and receives something else, raising TypeError or ValueError lets the caller handle or log the problem immediately. Try to write clear messages and choose the most specific built-in exception available.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 3 › What raise Does
Definition

raise: explicit error signaling

Raise stops execution and produces an exception object. Use it for input validation and business-rule enforcement so callers can catch and handle the problem.

Check type and range early and raise the appropriate built-in exception.
Include clear messages to explain why the error occurred.
Avoid raising the generic base Exception; prefer specific exceptions.
Key Takeaway

Raise makes function contracts explicit and produces predictable, catchable errors.

Example
def calculate_positive_square_root(number):
    if not isinstance(number, (int, float)):
        raise TypeError("Input must be a number (int or float).")
    if number < 0:
        raise ValueError("Cannot calculate square root of a negative number.")
    return number ** 0.5

try:
    print(calculate_positive_square_root(25))
    print(calculate_positive_square_root(-9))
except ValueError as e:
    print(f"Caught an error: {e}")
Misconception
raise is not only for fatal errors; it is for predictable, expected problem cases you want callers to handle.
Pro tip
Pick the most specific built-in exception available to make handling precise.

screens.title: Raising Built-in Exceptions with Clear Messages
screens.narratorSegment: Using built-in exceptions is a fast and communicative way to report common problems. TypeError is appropriate when a caller passes a value of the wrong type; ValueError is appropriate when the type is correct but the value is out of acceptable range. A common pattern is to validate inputs at the top of a function and raise immediately with a helpful message. The example code shows a function that checks both types and ranges before computing a result. When you raise built-ins this way, exception handlers higher in the program can choose to recover or present a clear error to users. A typical misuse is raising a generic Exception type, which makes it harder for callers to distinguish different failure modes. Always include concise messages that state the condition and, when helpful, the offending value. This improves logging and debugging. Think about who will handle the exception: a library should document and raise clear exception types so callers can write targeted handlers. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 6 › Chapter 3 › Built-in Exceptions
Code Walkthrough

Validate types and values early

Early checks make failures precise and place the responsibility on the caller to supply valid inputs.

def validate_age(age_value):
    if not isinstance(age_value, int):
        raise TypeError("Age must be an integer.")
    if not (0 <= age_value <= 120):
        raise ValueError("Age must be between 0 and 120, inclusive.")
    print(f"Age set to: {age_value}")

try:
    validate_age(30)
    validate_age(-5)
except (TypeError, ValueError) as e:
    print(f"Error setting age: {e}")
Why messages matter
A precise message helps the caller and logs explain exactly what to fix without guessing.
Misuse to avoid
Don't use a bare generic Exception; it prevents selective except clauses that handle specific problems.
Checklist
  • Decide whether the error is type-based or value-based.
  • Raise the corresponding built-in with a short message.
  • Document which exceptions your function may raise.
Key Takeaway

Clear, specific built-in exceptions improve error handling and debugging.

screens.title: Custom Exception Classes
screens.narratorSegment: Custom exceptions let you represent domain-specific failure modes clearly. Instead of relying only on built-in types, create a small class that inherits from Exception or from a relevant built-in subclass. This allows calling code to catch that specific error and react differently than it would to a ValueError or TypeError. A simple custom class can add attributes — for example, storing the invalid temperature value — so error handlers can access extra context without parsing messages. The pattern is intentionally lightweight: define the class, optionally add an initializer that stores context, then raise that class when a domain rule is violated. The chapter includes an InvalidTemperatureError that inherits from ValueError and stores the offending temperature. A common misconception is that custom exceptions are heavy; in fact they are a small, readable addition that improves clarity and allows granular except clauses in larger code bases. Module 6 › Chapter 3 › Custom Exceptions
Definition

Make domain errors explicit

Custom exceptions allow callers to write targeted handlers and to carry structured context about the error.

Inherit from Exception or a related built-in type for semantics.
Add attributes in __init__ to store extra context like the invalid value.
When to create one
  • You need to handle a specific error differently from built-ins.
  • Errors include extra context that handlers should read programmatically.
  • Clarity for API users: documentation can list the custom exception type.
Analogy

Think of custom exceptions as labeled warning flags. A generic flag tells you something failed; a labeled flag tells you exactly which rule failed and how to recover.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 3 › InvalidTemperatureError
Code Example
class InvalidTemperatureError(ValueError):
    """Raised when a temperature value is outside a valid range."""
    def __init__(self, message="Temperature is outside valid range", temperature=None):
        super().__init__(message)
        self.temperature = temperature

def set_room_temperature(temp):
    if not isinstance(temp, (int, float)):
        raise TypeError("Temperature must be a number.")
    if not (18 <= temp <= 25):
        raise InvalidTemperatureError(f"Temperature {temp}°C is not within the acceptable range (18-25°C).", temp)
    print(f"Room temperature set to {temp}°C.")

try:
    set_room_temperature(22)
    set_room_temperature(15)
except InvalidTemperatureError as e:
    print(f"Custom error caught: {e}. Invalid temperature was: {e.temperature}")
Handler benefit
The handler can access e.temperature directly, avoiding brittle message parsing.
Notes
  • Inherit from a relevant built-in to keep semantics intuitive.
  • Keep exceptions lightweight: store context, avoid heavy logic.
  • Document the custom exception so callers know to catch it.
Common mistake

Adding behavior to exception classes makes them harder to serialize or handle; prefer simple context storage.

screens.title: The assert Statement
screens.narratorSegment: Assert is a lightweight way to state an assumption your code relies on. You write assert followed by a condition and an optional message; if the condition is false Python raises AssertionError with your message. Use assert for developer-facing conditions that should never fail during correct execution, such as an internal invariant after a filtering step. For example, after filtering a list you might assert it is not empty to catch a bug in the filtering logic. Important: assertions can be disabled at runtime when Python is run with optimizations, so they should not be used for validating user input or other checks that must always run. A common mistake is using assert where raise should be used; remember that raise expresses an expected error mode that production code must enforce, while assert is a guard against programming mistakes during development. Use short messages that help identify the violated invariant when tests fail. The assert Statement means use assert to capture invariants during testing; don't rely on it for critical runtime validation because it can be disabled.. In practical terms, developer-facing sanity checks for internal consistency. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Module 6 › Chapter 3 › assert Statement
Definition

assert condition, optional message

Assert raises AssertionError if its condition is false. Use it for internal checks that indicate a bug if violated.

Assertions may be disabled with optimization flags, so do not use for essential validation.
Good for catching developer mistakes during testing and debugging.
Example
def divide(a, b):
    assert b != 0, "Denominator cannot be zero!"
    return a / b

print(divide(10, 2))
# print(divide(10, 0)) would raise AssertionError
After input validation, assertions act as final sanity checks to catch bugs early. Remember that they can be turned off.
Misuse to avoid
Do not use assert to validate user input such as form fields. Those checks must run in production and should use explicit raise and if statements.
Key Takeaway

Assert documents developer expectations; use raise for production validation.

screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the difference between raise and assert is central to writing robust code. Raise is used to announce expected errors that are part of normal program interaction: bad input, unavailable resources, or business-rule violations. These should be handled with try-except blocks and must remain active in production. Assert is a development-time statement to ensure your internal logic is correct; if an assertion fails it signals a bug that should be fixed by the developer. A key practical difference is that asserts can be disabled when Python runs with optimizations, so you cannot rely on them for essential validation. A typical scenario: use raise to check an A P I input's type and range, then use assert after your own validation to confirm an invariant you expect to hold. content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 3 › raise vs assert
raise

Production checks

Used for expected error conditions like invalid user input or missing resources. Always active and should be handled by callers.

  • Type and value validation
  • Business rule violations
  • Caught and handled with try-except
assert

Developer sanity checks

Used to catch logic bugs during development. Can be disabled with optimization flags and should not replace runtime validation.

  • Document internal invariants
  • Signals a bug if violated
  • Not guaranteed to run in production
Guideline
If a check must always run for correctness or security, use raise. If it documents an assumption that helps developers detect bugs, use assert.
Common mistake

Using assert for user input validation can silently fail in optimized runs, creating security or correctness holes.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Best Practices
screens.narratorSegment: There are predictable errors programmers make when using raise and assert. First, treating assert as input validation risks disabling critical checks when Python runs optimized. Second, raising overly generic Exception types makes it hard for callers to respond appropriately. Third, embedding heavy logic or side effects in exception classes complicates handling and serialization. Module 6 › Chapter 3 › place_order Activity
Starter Code
class InsufficientStockError(ValueError):
    """Custom exception raised when requested quantity exceeds available stock."""
    pass

def place_order(product_name, quantity, available_stock):
    # Input validation using 'raise'
    if not isinstance(quantity, int) or not isinstance(available_stock, int):
        raise TypeError("Quantity and available stock must be integers.")

    if quantity <= 0:
        raise ValueError("Order quantity must be a positive integer.")

    if available_stock < 0:
        raise ValueError("Available stock cannot be negative.")

    if quantity > available_stock:
        raise InsufficientStockError(
            f"Cannot order {quantity} units of {product_name}. Only {available_stock} available."
        )

    assert quantity > 0 and available_stock >= quantity, \
        "Internal logic error: quantity or stock validation failed unexpectedly."

    print(f"Successfully placed order for {quantity} units of {product_name}.")
    print(f"Remaining stock for {product_name}: {available_stock - quantity}")
Run the test calls to observe each exception being raised and caught. The assert guards against programming errors in the validation logic itself.
Test Cases
  1. Valid order: place_order("Laptop", 2, 10)
  2. Insufficient stock: place_order("Mouse", 5, 3)
  3. Invalid quantity: place_order("Keyboard", 0, 5)
  4. Negative stock: place_order("Monitor", 1, -2)
  5. Wrong type: place_order("Webcam", "one", 5)

Combine explicit raises with a final assert to document both external validation and internal invariants.

fullNarratorScript:
In this short module you'll learn when your program should explicitly signal an error and when to use internal checks. We start with the raise keyword, which lets your code deliberately throw an exception when input or business rules are violated. You will see how raising built-in exceptions makes a function's contract clear, and how defining your own exception classes helps larger applications distinguish error types. Then we'll cover the assert statement, which is intended for developer-facing sanity checks and can be disabled in optimized runs. Along the way you'll study practical examples like validating an age or temperature, implement a custom InsufficientStockError for order logic, and try a hands-on activity that mixes raise and assert correctly. Why this matters: explicit errors make programs more predictable and maintainable, while assertions help catch bugs early. Consider how you would want errors reported in a small script versus a production service—this lesson helps you choose the right tool.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to intentionally signal error conditions, choose between built-in and custom exception types, and use assertions to check internal program state. First, you will learn when to use the raise statement to stop execution with a clear error if input or business rules are violated. Second, you will differentiate raising standard exceptions like ValueError or TypeError from creating small custom classes that inherit from Exception, which helps callers catch domain-specific problems. Third, you will implement the assert statement as a debugging tool to verify invariants that should always hold. Finally, you will understand the lifecycle difference: raise is for production checks you expect to handle, while assert is for developer-facing checks that may be disabled in optimized runs. Each objective includes a brief example and a milestone that verifies competency.

You will learn to implement input validation using raise, to design a small custom exception class that carries extra information, and to write assert statements that validate program invariants after your checks. The exercises include a place_order function that raises TypeError, ValueError, or a custom InsufficientStockError, and then uses assert as a final internal check. The raise statement tells Python to stop normal execution and create an exception object representing an error you determined has occurred. Use raise when a function receives inputs or conditions that violate the intended contract. When you raise a built-in exception, you can include a short explanatory message to help callers and debuggers understand what happened. A common pattern is input validation at the start of a function: check types and ranges, then raise TypeError or ValueError as appropriate. Why this matters: without explicit raises your code might continue into invalid states and cause misleading errors later, making bugs harder to trace. A common misconception is treating raise as only for catastrophic failures; in reality, it's the right tool for predictable, catchable problems. Example: if a function expects a positive integer and receives something else, raising TypeError or ValueError lets the caller handle or log the problem immediately.
